🟡 Sinal do Vale

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website

Sinal do Vale runs a bioregional hub in Brazil's Atlantic Rainforest, serving as a catalyst for regeneration through community-based entrepreneurship and systems integration.

Once rich in biodiversity and cultural significance, the bay now faces severe pollution from untreated sewage, industrial waste, and urban runoff.

Background


Guanabara Bay is one of Brasil's largest and most iconic coastal ecosystems, framed by the Atlantic Forest and surrounded by one of the world's most densely populated urban areas. Once rich in biodiversity and cultural significance, the bay now faces severe pollution from untreated sewage, industrial waste, and urban runoff.

For over 15 years, Sinal do Vale has earned the trust and reputation in this bioregion—situated in the buffer zone between Rio de Janeiro and the Mata Atlântica rainforest. The beautiful Mata Atlântica has incredible biodiversity, but has already lost 88% of its size to date. This bioregion delivers the water, food, and other ecosystem services for Rio and surrounding areas, yet it faces urban encroachment, loss of rivers, and low economic activity leading to poverty.

Origins and Network


Against that backdrop, Sinal do Vale set out years ago to show how a biohub can act as a catalyst inside a bioregion and help grow a bioeconomy.

After 15 years of strong results on very limited budgets, the organization is now working toward self-sufficiency so it can sustain and expand that work for the bioregion.

Activities

🔸

Biocultural Hub

The site functions as a bioregional hub: a place where visitors, partners, and local actors meet, learn, and test ideas. It has developed into an internationally renowned UN Flagship Biohub—combining learning journeys, hospitality, and living prototypes of bioeconomic enterprise so regeneration is visible and repeatable, not only discussed. Two lines of work help keep the hub viable: Sinal do Vale’s own hospitality offer and the Madre Frutas social enterprise (below), which together connect revenue, training, and on-the-ground demonstration.

🔸

Madre Frutas Social Enterprise

Madre Frutas is a women-led enterprise that turns abundant local jackfruit into marketable products. It models agro-processing tied to regenerative practice, women’s leadership, and economic resilience—creating livelihoods where options are scarce while respecting what the land already provides.

🔸

Camino do Guaraú Eco-Tourism Trail

The 110-kilometer trail starts not by coincidence at Sinal do Vale. By curating this officially recognized Camino do Guaraú, Sinal do Vale galvanized entrepreneurs, activists, change makers, and farmers to join the regeneration movement. The trail reconnects the local community to its heritage, culture, and ecotourism potential. The trail continues through nine other segments in the beautiful mountain range of the Mata Atlântica. In each segment, Sinal do Vale has identified areas that need reforestation or conservation to create an agroecological belt to preserve and regenerate the biodiversity in the region. Not least among the species they're working to protect: the golden lion tamarin monkeys, an endangered species that depends on the health of this ecosystem. This work is about creating connected corridors of life, ensuring that the fragments of the Mata Atlântica can support the full diversity of life they once sustained.

🔸

Val Estrela Historic and Cultural Ecotourism Site

After about 20 kilometers through great landscapes, the trail arrives at Val Estrela—the port where one-third of the slaves arrived in Brazil. This is a site of profound historical and cultural significance, and Sinal do Vale has started executing a master plan to regenerate the rivers, the old church, and weighing station to create a historic and cultural ecotourism site. They're doing this work together with the local quilombola communities and fishermen who maintained this abandoned site over the past decades. These are communities with deep ancestral connections to this place, who have been stewarding it even as it was neglected by broader society. Sinal do Vale is determined to continue this work, recognizing that restoration must honor both the ecological and cultural heritage of this place.

🔸

Terra Umida Agroforestry Corridor

Another 30 kilometers along the trail, hikers pass wide degraded farmlands called Terra Umida. This is a government-supported area where the landless farmer movement of Brazil is working under very tough conditions to regenerate degraded land through agroforestry. Sinal do Vale has started building new supply chains for the farmer and food sector, seeing the potential to build a true bioeconomy with these farmers to benefit their livelihoods. This is about rebuilding food systems, forming regenerative supply chains with local producers, and creating economic pathways that align with ecological restoration.

🔸

SINAL Flow Fund

The SINAL Flow Fund is a locally managed funding mechanism designed to channel diverse capital streams—including public grants, donations, supply chain finance, and investment capital—toward regenerative initiatives in the region. The Flow Fund enables implementation of community-led projects by lowering access barriers to funding and supporting infrastructure for scaling a bioregional economy.

Vision and Legacy


What Sinal do Vale demonstrates is how a biohub can be a catalyst that creates the conditions for regeneration to flourish across an entire bioregion. For over 15 years, working with very limited financial resources yet achieving amazing results, they've shown what's possible when you anchor action in place, build trust with communities, and weave connections across scales from individual projects to regional bioeconomy.

From the women turning jackfruit into livelihoods at Madre Frutas to the quilombola communities restoring Val Estrela, from the landless farmers regenerating Terra Umida through agroforestry to the protection of golden lion tamarins in the Mata Atlântica—Sinal do Vale is showing how supply chains of value can regenerate landscapes that are so important for culture, for people, and for the web of life that connects us all.
